Michael Moritz on the Time profile that ended his relationship with Steve Jobs, and whether he was ever in awe of him.

"Steve was convinced that he was going to be named Man of the Year, even though nobody had told him that. 

But worst of all, the profile, which he hated for very good reason, and I was appalled by for different reasons, severed my relationship with Steve. 

Back then at Time, these things went through an editorial combine harvester. 

So what came out in the bale at the end probably didn't resemble very much of the straw that got fed in. And so the whole tone of the piece was malicious and nasty and underhanded. 

Sadly, as a result of that, really never repaired the relationship with Steve.

Were you in awe of him? 

No.

I respected him. I admired him tremendously. But I knew some of the darker shades of him, which made it difficult to hold him up as an object of unalloyed admiration. But he's a heroic figure, obviously."

Sad to see Balancer winding down:

I have fond memories using (and farming) it since day 1 but tbh I haven't used it for years now. So shutting down is understandable.

Interestingly, if the proposal passes, holders could redeem $BAL for their share of the treasury.

~$9.15M treasury vs ~$7.6M market cap.

Without treasury held $BAL and shutdown costs and we get ~11% upside at current prices. Still need to confirm how much BAL qualifies.

And unclaimed allocations go to those who redeem!

If 10% of eligible BAL goes unclaimed, the payout per redeemed token rises another ~11%.

So lost keys could benefit everyone else. I bet smart traders already calculating the trade.

But redemptions only start in May 2027, with unclaimed shares distributed by January 2028.

Quite a wait for that spread and lock in your capital...

My conversation with Michael Moritz, one of the great venture investors of the last 40 years. 

Michael joined Sequoia in 1986 and co-led the firm with Doug Leone (@dougleone) from 1995 to 2012. His investments include Google, Yahoo, PayPal, and Stripe.

His new book, Ausländer, traces his parents' escape from Nazi Germany and helps explain his lifelong interest in what shapes exceptional people.

We discuss:
- The infamous Steve Jobs profile
- Why Don Valentine hired him
- The question he finds most revealing when interviewing people
- Monomania and the cost of greatness
- Why he has never felt good at anything
- Writing, journalism and AI
- What he learned about himself writing Ausländer

I'd recommend watching this one if you can. Michael was incredibly thoughtful and reflective throughout, particularly when talking about his parents, childhood, and the more difficult parts of his personal story.

Enjoy!

All this underscores just how difficult it is to evolve a Fed–market paradigm anchored by years of handholding, a constant stream of official commentary, excessive backward-looking data dependency, and a forward guidance regime that stumbled into spurious accuracy.
More to follow.
#economy #markets #federalreserve

There's currently a cambrian explosion of innovative onchain mechanisms

We're only just scratching the surface of how distributed systems can be used to leverage the "Wisdom of Crowds"

@umia_finance launched its UMIA token recently & will be incubating a number of high quality projects that'll be coming through its pipeline

But something I'm paying closer attention to the ongoing decision making & how these onchain mechanisms play into that process

Crypto made capital formation permissionless but left "control" of the capital largely unchanged

Teams sell tokens, take custody of the treasury, keep the IP inside a separate company & can treat token governance as advisory, with no consequences for ignoring outcomes

Tokenholders finance the business while remaining structurally downstream of it

Umia puts major project decisions through "conditional markets"; large treasury spend, acquisition, new issuance or strategic pivot creates two or more markets: 

i) one (or more) where the proposal passes, and; 
ii) a No-Op market where nothing changes

Traders price the project’s token under both futures & the proposal only executes if its TWAP beats the status quo by a defined threshold

This bit is super interesting to me because of the “Wisdom of Crowds” I mentioned above; it has somewhat been proven out in elections using prediction markets which have turned out to be more accurate than your average poll

Imagine a public company creating two temporary versions of its stock for every major board decision: 

i) one pricing the company if the deal happens, and; 
ii) one if it does not

The market that sustains the higher valuation determines what the company does...

Founders remain the C-suite, the market acts as the board, the treasury contract controls the money and the legal structure binds the development team to the outcome

This closes one of crypto’s largest structural gaps: linking tokenholder capital to enforceable control over how it’s used

The Clarity Act may have stalled yesterday, but pay attention to onchain mechanisms that enhance the ownership rights of tokenized businesses... it'll become increasingly important

One thing I didn't focus on enough in my last post about @TrezuApp is the lack of commercial confidentiality in crypto.

Once someone links a wallet to your company, they can start estimating your budgets, salaries, contractor payments, or even how much runway you have left.

That can give contractors leverage in negotiations and competitors insight into how your business operates.

Essentially, Trezu lets teams hold crypto, pay employees and contractors, swap tokens, and manage payment approvals in one place, with the option to keep your finances private.

Governance stays public and verifiable. Finances stay private.

With Confidential Treasuries, anyone can see the multisig members and that a vote took place, but they can't see how much money the treasury holds or who the team is paying.

The confidential treasury runs on a private shard on @NEARProtocol, letting teams:

→ Keep treasury balances private
→ Keep payment proposals visible only to the team
→ Pay contractors in batches with multisig approvals

And when you pay a contractor’s public wallet, the money arrives from a generic NEAR Intents address. Someone checking that wallet would see a transfer from a smart contract, without a direct public link back to your company’s treasury.

So if you’re managing company funds onchain, you can create a confidential treasury for free: https://t.co/IlP1eO86JE

I find this more interesting than another standard meme launcher, though it depends on whether tokenized stocks actually gain traction on the chain.

@Arguspad is a straightforward memecoin launchpad. I’m watching whether it starts producing actual runners.

One or two successful launches can change where traders spend their time, but I’d want to see that happen before getting too excited about $ARGUS.

4. Warp ($WARP): Cross-chain USDC launchpad

@circlewarp combines a launchpad and trading terminal with cross-chain USDC transfers through CCTP.

The appeal is being able to move USDC from another chain and trade tokens on Arc without going through three different apps.

@Archemistdotfun lets you launch tokens through an X bot. Its V4 setup includes anti-snipe mechanics, creator buys, buybacks and holder rewards.

I’m curious how the anti-snipe mechanics work in practice once people are trading with real money.

If launches end up spread across 20 different venues, having somewhere to see what’s moving would save a lot of digging.

Do you like $INTC ?

I believe Intel has had several significant positive developments over the past month. The stock appears to have bottomed around $85 and now trades near $97.

Yesterday, I opened the following trade, which expires on November 20:

Buy one $95 call.
Sell three $130 calls.
Sell one $80 put.

The maximum profit is around $130, meaning Intel would need to rise approximately 33% by November 20. On the downside, I only start losing if Intel falls more than 20%, at which point I would be assigned the shares at $80. On the upside, the trade remains profitable unless Intel rises more than approximately 51% from that point you start loosing money.

My logic is as follows: 

1) We are entering a period of weak seasonality, which is usually a difficult time for the stock market. That is one reason I feel comfortable selling the three $130 calls, I intentionally want to waste time.

2) On the other hand, Intel has had several positive developments recently. That is why I also feel comfortable selling the $80 put.

That is the basic logic behind the trade: I am positive on Intel, but I am not expecting an extreme move higher by November 20. The sweet spot is a ~35% rise in the next 66 days, with the maximum profit around $130.

You could also view this trade as an add-on to an existing Intel position. Let’s say Intel currently represents 5% of your portfolio. If the stock rises “only” to $130, you will make money on both the options and the stock. If it rises 50% to $150, you will still be very happy because of the profit on your shares, despite not making money on the options trade.

If Intel falls to $80, perhaps that is a price at which you would feel comfortable doubling your position. You receive additional shares at a price you like and continue holding them because you believe Intel should perform well over the long term.

Remember, this is just an idea, not a recommendation. You might want to choose different strikes or expiration.

-Warm intros drafted from a network of 15,000+ contacts

-Answers to any question from our own records in plain English across 400+ portfolio companies (and an extra info assist from our Harmonic API)

The AI/ML infrastructure handles the routine work, but judgment remains human: sitting across from a founder, recognizing a missionary, making the call while the idea still sounds crazy.
